doc_name: Risen Christ (Michelangelo, Santa Maria sopra Minerva)
text: The Risen Christ (Cristo della Minerva in Italian, also known as Christ the Redeemer or Christ Carrying the Cross) is a marble sculpture by the Italian High Renaissance master Michelangelo, completed in 1521. It is located in the church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome, to the left of the main altar. The work was commissioned in June 1514 by the Roman patrician Metello Vari, who specified only that the nude standing figure should hold the Cross in his arms, leaving the composition entirely to Michelangelo. Michelangelo began a first version in his studio at Macello dei Corvi around 1515 but abandoned it in roughed-out condition after discovering a black vein in the white marble, a detail noted by Vari in a letter and later by Ulisse Aldrovandi. A new version was quickly prepared between 1519 and 1520 to meet the contract terms. Michelangelo worked on it in Florence, with the move to Rome and final touches entrusted to apprentice Pietro Urbano, who damaged the work and was replaced by Federico Frizzi at the suggestion of Sebastiano del Piombo. The first version, though unfinished, was given to Metello Vari in January 1522 for his palazzetto near Santa Maria sopra Minerva, described as "As his greatest honor, as if it were of gold," reflecting the high esteem for Michelangelo. It remained there, was noted by Aldrovandi in 1556, and was reportedly for sale in 1607 before going missing. In 2000, Irene Baldriga identified the lost first version in the sacristy of the church of San Vincenzo Martire, near Viterbo, where the black vein is clearly visible on Christ's left cheek; it is now known as the Giustiniani Christ. The later additions include the "right hand, parts of the face, and the back." Despite these challenges, the second version made a strong impression on contemporaries, with Sebastiano del Piombo declaring that the knees alone were worthy of more than the whole of Rome—a praise William Wallace has called "one of the most curious praises ever sung about a work of art." Christ is depicted nude in a standing pose, with exposed sexual organs intended to symbolize his uncorrupted sexuality and complete control over his will, thus demonstrating his triumph over sin and death. A floating bronze loincloth was added in 1546 to cover the genitals. The second version features a flexed leg and a turned-back head, following the principle of contrapposto, allowing a more dynamic and varied impression from different angles, "not only activating the space around him, but also suggesting an unfolding story." The first version was exhibited in the National Gallery, London in 2017, alongside a cast of the second version, drawings for it, and letters related to it.
